Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA corner Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City http: //www.dilg.com.ph DILG OPINION No. 41 s. 2023 MAY 2023 HON. CHRISTIAN G. LAO Vice-Mayor, Municipality of Allen Northern Samar Dear Vice-Mayor Lao: This refers to your letter dated January 23, 2023, seeking this Department's legal opinion concerning the validity of an ordinance—entitled "Appropriation Ordinance No. 22-s-2022, intending for this purpose to appropriating the amount of One Hundred Million Twenty-Eight Million Six Hundred Eighty-One Thousand Four Hundred Thirty- Three Pesos and Ninety-Two Centavos (Php 128,681,433.91)"—passed by the 19th Sangguniang Bayan during its 3rd Special Session. As represented in your letter, the said ordinance was enacted on December 23, 2022. It was approved by six (6) members of the herein concerned sanggunian; four (4) members were absent; and one (1) member abstained from signing the ordinance. Premised from the foregoing, arose your query: whether the passage of the subject ordinance in question is valid as it was only passed by six sangguniang members. At the outset, we deemed it apt to succinctly touch on what constitutes "majority" in the context of the legislative process. The term "majority" has been jurisprudentially defined as that which is greater than half of the membership of the body or that number which is 50% + 1 of the entire membership. Along this line, it is crucial to note that there are two (2) types of majorities in this context, i.e., simple majority and qualified majority—and the distinction between these two has been well established in our previous opinions. The former is defined as that which is the maiority_ of the members present, there being a quorum. Generally, ordinary measures—pertaining to the normal transactions of the sanggunian—require for their enactment only the approval of this type of majority. The latter is defined as that which is the majority of all duly elected and qualified members of the Sanggunian. regardless of whether all of them are present or not in a particular session. In a nutshell, it is one wherein the total membership of the sanggunian is considered in determining a majority. There are certain measures where the Local Government Code explicitly requires the approval or vote of this type of majority; for example, an ordinance creating liability. With the foregoing in mind, this now beckons the question: What type of majority is applicable in the present case? Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan" Trunkline No.: 8876-34-54

Relevant to this is our opinion in DILG Legal Opinion No. 13, s. 2010. In it, we opined that a simple majority is required for the enactment of annual and supplemental appropriations. Our view is anchored on our observations that the law is silent as to what kind of majority vote is required for annual and supplemental ordinances. Thus, in its silence, the presumption is that the same is to be enacted only by a simple majority. To bolster this, Article 107 of the Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of the Local Government Code of 1991 (Republic Act No. 7160) expressly provides that: "ARTICLE 107. Ordinances and Resolutions. — The following rules shall govern the enactment of ordinances and resolutions: Xxx (g) No ordinance or resolution passed by the sanggunian in a regular or special session duly called for the purpose shall be valid unless approved by a maioritv of the members present, there being a quorum. Any ordinance or resolution authorizing or directing the payment of money or creating liability, shall require the affirmative vote of a majority of all sangunian members for its passage." (Emphasis supplied) From the foregoing provision, it could be gathered that the general rule is that an ordinance or resolution should only be approved by a majority of the members of the sanggunian present, there being a quorum. The exception provided by the IRR is that when it directs a payment of money or creates liability, the required vote is a qualified majority. In the present case, there appears to be a total of twelve (12) members, including the Presiding Officer. Here, it is crucial to first determine whether a quorum was attained in this particular session. A quorum is defined by Section 53 of the Local Government Code as referring to the presence of the majority of all the members of the sanggunian who have been duly elected and qualified (DILG Legal Opinion No. 13, s. 2010). Accordingly, 12 members, including the presiding officer, the quorum should be computed in this manner: 12/2=6 (is the 50%) 6+1=7 Hence, the total number required to constitute a quorum is 7. As represented, seven members—excluding the Vice-Mayor—were present during the session. Clearly, there was a quorum. Having established the foregoing, we now address the crucial question: whether the six sangguniang members who voted in favor of the subject ordinance in question should suffice to muster the required majority—or, to be more accurate, a simple majority. Applying the foregoing discussions on simple majority, four (4) out of seven (7) members present during the session are the required number of votes to validly pass the subject ordinance: 3.5 (50% of 7) + 1 = 4.5, or only 4 because it is more than 50%. Page 2 of 2

In view of the foregoing, it appears that the herein concerned sanggunian has validly obtained the required number of majority in the approval of the subject ordinance in question, with a vote of 6 in favor thereof. This opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities and the courts. We hope to have guided you accordingly. Thank you. Very truly yours, By the utho y of the Secretary: ATT . JU V CTOR R. LLAMAS Underse etary for External, Legal and Legislative Affairs OUSEL VULLLS-LRALLD1ja DIR. ARNEL M.
